alignment.note: Greek ἐνδιδύσκουσιν (3rd plural finite verb) and Latin induunt are matched by the Syriac single inflected form ܘܐܠܒܫܘܗܝ, which incorporates both the conjunction ('and'), the verb (l-b-sh, 'to clothe'), and the 3rd-masculine-singular object suffix ('him'). The Syriac thus collapses what the Greek and Latin express analytically with a separate object pronoun.

The accusative object αὐτὸν / eum ('him') is rendered in Syriac not as a free pronoun but as the verbal suffix on ܘܐܠܒܫܘܗܝ; there is no discrete Peshitta token to align, reflecting the synthetic morphology of Syriac.
πορφύραν / ܐܪܓܘܢܐ / purpura — the garment of imperial purple. The Syriac ܐܪܓܘܢܐ is a loanword (cf. Greek ἀργεμώνη / Akkadian argamannu), not derived from a native root despite the listed r-g-n.

Greek and Latin position the participle πλέξαντες / plectentes ('having twisted/plaited') after the main verb of placing, whereas the Syriac fronts ܘܓܕܠܘ (g-d-l, 'and they plaited') as a coordinate finite verb before the act of placing. Syriac favors paratactic coordinate verbs over the Greek subordinating aorist participle.
περιτιθέασιν / ܣܡܘ / imponunt — 'they set/place upon.' The Syriac s-m ('to set') is more general than the Greek περιτίθημι ('place around'), but contextually equivalent.

ἀκάνθινον / ܕܟܘܒܐ / spineam — 'of thorns.' Greek and Latin use an adjective ('thorny'), while Syriac employs a genitive noun phrase ܕܟܘܒܐ ('of thorn[s]'), a construction-level rather than lexical difference.
